**Architect's countermeasure**: Calibrate the simulator on the bench before randomizing, record whether each range comes from a physical measurement or from a success-driven curriculum such as automatic domain randomization, and log omitted mechanisms in the policy manifest's omission log, retaining only operating conditions that independent limits can cover under validated physical assumptions.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Assuming multi-step generative decoders can execute synchronously within inner actuator control loops.*\index{Diffusion policy!inference latency wall}

An ML engineer proposes replacing `latch-bc-01`'s one-pass ACT decoder with a `{python} DecoderBudget.k_ddim_str`-step diffusion head, having observed better multimodal trajectory modeling in offline benchmarks, and runs it synchronously, one inference per `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_step_str` setpoint. Under the budget of @sec-training-decoder-costs, the stipulated complete inference takes `{python} DecoderBudget.t_ddim_str`, longer than the step, so the synchronous schedule drops setpoints, and the execution path must either hold the last admitted setpoint or invoke its fallback on every overrun. Checking only the weight-streaming floor of @sec-brain-memory-wall would not have caught this: that floor is a lower bound, not a latency measurement, and a decoder can fail its deadline while passing it. **A decoder that overruns its deadline needs fewer evaluations, a different implementation, or asynchronous execution under an independently validated lease.**

**Architect's countermeasure**: Decouple iterative inference from inner actuator execution when the measured decoder latency requires it. Record the prediction horizon, executed prefix, proposal-renewal deadline, and active lease separately under the qualified contract of @sec-nervous-lease-sizing. Buffering does not extend permission: the execution path checks current evidence and state and invokes its qualified fallback on expiry.

:::

## Summary {#sec-training-summary}

Every training regime buys a capability and leaves a dependency in the weights. Behavioral cloning depends on the states its demonstrators visited and can average incompatible action choices; offline value learning cannot reach states its log never visited; post-training a pretrained generalist borrows competence but no supported cell; learning by trial on the machine spends calendar time, heat, and component life; simulation depends on its contact model, timing, and omitted mechanisms; fine-tuning depends on recent experience and requires evidence for the updated checkpoint. Whatever the regime, its decoder must also meet the machine's proposal deadline, and a more expressive action distribution earns no extra time at the actuator. A training score alone does not expose those dependencies. Tracing each one to a possible failure identifies what evaluation must test and what independent execution limits must cover. Principle \ref{pri-vol4-endogenous-drift} requires attention to the states a policy's own corrections reach, while simulation adds a second kind of absence, the mechanisms its solver never represented. The policy manifest records that reasoning and confines the declared operating domain accordingly. For the latch, it sends `latch-bc-01` to evaluation at the nominal plate and the guarded approach, and keeps the simulation-refined checkpoints out of service until paired probes close their omissions, because an action admitted on the strength of a training score crosses the causal boundary with only that score behind it.

@Tbl-06-key-equations collects the equations that carry these decisions, what each bounds or decides, and where each is derived.

| Equation                                                                                                                                | What it bounds or decides                                                                                            | Derived in                          |
|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------|
| $\pi^*(\mathbf{o}) = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{a} \mid \mathbf{o}]$                                                                            | The squared-error optimum of a point-regression policy, which lies between demonstrated modes                        | @eq-training-mse-minimizer          |
| $Q^\pi(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{a}) = r(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{a}) + \gamma\,\mathbb{E}[Q^\pi(\mathbf{s}', \mathbf{a}')]$                       | The value recursion that offline and policy-gradient learning estimate from samples                                  | @eq-training-bellman                |
| $t_{\text{infer}} = t_{\text{enc}} + \sum_{k=1}^{N_{\text{eval}}} t_{\text{pass}} \le t_{\text{deadline}}$                              | Whether a decoder fits the setpoint step synchronously or the renewal period asynchronously                          | @eq-training-decoder-latency        |
| $T_{\text{wall}} = N\,(t_{\text{rollout}} + t_{\text{reset}})/N_{\text{rig}}$                                                           | The calendar of a physical training campaign, which rigs divide but wear does not follow                             | @eq-training-trial-wall-clock       |
| $F_{\text{peak}} = v\sqrt{k\,m}$                                                                                                        | The peak force of a mass coasting into a contact, which a soft penalty spring understates                            | @eq-training-impact-peak            |
| $k_{\text{eff}} = (1/k_{\text{plate}} + 1/k_{\text{robot}})^{-1}$                                                                       | The robot-side stiffness above which a coasting approach exceeds the latch limit                                     | @eq-training-series-stiffness       |
| $t_{\text{yield}} = F_{\text{lim}}/(k v)$                                                                                               | The time from touch to the force limit under constant drive, which confines the declared ODD to the guarded approach | @eq-training-contact-yield-deadline |
| $J_{\text{DR}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\xi} \sim p(\boldsymbol{\xi})}[J(\boldsymbol{\theta}; \boldsymbol{\xi})]$ | Return averaged over the parameters a simulator models, never over mechanisms it omits                               | @eq-training-dr-objective           |
| $\mathbf{u}_{\text{prop}} = \pi_{\text{base}} + g(\mathbf{s})\,\Delta\pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$                                         | Where a learned residual may act, and so what the regression evidence must cover                                     | @eq-training-gated-residual         |

: **Key equations of policy training**: Each load-bearing equation of the chapter, the limit it bounds or the decision it settles, and the equation where it is derived. {#tbl-06-key-equations tbl-colwidths="[40,42,18]"}

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Policy synthesis and sim-to-real transfer"}
* **Every regime leaves a dependency no training score shows:** Offline loss and simulated return reward compliance with the data and the solver. Candidate rankings can therefore invert on hardware, and a deployment condition that violates a dependency produces a predictable failure signature that names the detector the permission path needs.
* **Mode choice and recovery are separate problems:** Regression can average valid alternatives into an invalid action, while successive errors can reach states the demonstrations omit. A multimodal decoder addresses the first problem; recovery experience and closed-loop evidence address the second. Independent runtime limits remain necessary for both.
* **Decoder latency must fit the proposal contract:** Repeated model evaluations increase latency and memory traffic. When a decoder cannot meet the synchronous deadline, asynchronous chunk playback needs a validated lease and fallback. A more expressive action distribution does not earn extra time at the actuator.
* **Training information must survive the sensor boundary:** Privileged simulation state can guide learning, but the deployed student sees only its runtime inputs. Observation history helps only where different physical conditions leave distinguishable traces; distillation does not remove the need for calibration and transfer testing.
* **Randomization covers parameters, not missing mechanisms:** Domain randomization broadens training over dynamics the simulator already models, and paired probes size the remaining gap channel by channel. An omitted backlash, compliance, or transport delay stays omitted and enters the omission log.
* **Fine-tuning spends wear and reopens qualification:** Physical rollouts consume component life, and evidence collected for earlier weights does not automatically apply to the updated checkpoint. A gated residual limits where adaptation acts, but the combined controller still requires regression tests and independent execution limits.
* **A wider declared ODD needs new support:** The policy manifest cites the current data by digest and excludes conditions affected by unresolved omissions. Pretraining, simulator throughput, and learned world models add no supported cell. New attributable recovery experience can support a broader candidate domain; closed-loop qualification must establish the behavior claimed there.
:::

## Historical Perspective and Further Reading {#sec-training-history}

The reward formulation of this chapter descends from dynamic programming. @bellman1957dynamic gave the recursion that defines value, and @howard1960dynamic solved Markov decision processes by policy iteration. Learning from demonstration arrived by a separate route. ALVINN steered a vehicle from camera images by regressing on a driver's commands [@pomerleau1989alvinn], and the same system soon met the drift this chapter calls compounding error, because a network trained only on a careful driver's states never saw the off-center states its own errors produced [@pomerleau1991efficient]. @ross2011reduction turned that observation into a bound and an algorithm, DAgger, which gathers expert labels on the states the learner itself visits. The separate problem of averaging between valid demonstrations was answered by mixture models [@bishop1994mixture] and, for action chunks on real manipulators, by diffusion policies [@chi2024diffusionpolicy].

Policy-gradient methods date from REINFORCE [@williams1992simple], and value-based methods from Q-learning [@watkins1992q]. Neither prices a trial, and on a robot the trial is the dominant cost. Learning grasping from hundreds of thousands of real attempts [@levine2018learning; @kalashnikov2018qtopt] showed what that cost is in calendar time, hardware, and supervision, and the field's response was to move the trials into simulation. Proximal policy optimization became the default learner [@schulman2017ppo], and simulators resident on an accelerator made thousands of parallel rollouts routine [@makoviychuk2021isaac; @rudin2022learning].

Transfer then became the central problem. Domain randomization treated the real world as one more sample from a distribution of simulators [@tobin2017domain; @peng2018sim], and the Dactyl hand showed both what randomization and a recurrent policy could achieve and what the physical experiments still broke [@andrychowicz2020learning]. System identification, far older than any of these methods [@ljung1999system], returned in learned form as actuator networks [@hwangbo2019learning]. Generalist policies pretrained on pooled robot data [@kim2024openvla; @black2024pi0] moved the question again, from how to gather experience to what borrowed experience can be claimed as evidence. The policy manifest is this chapter's answer. It records each of these inheritances so that evaluation can test them.

For further reading, six works trace the path from dynamic programming to sim-to-real transfer.

- @sutton2018reinforcement develops Markov decision processes, value functions, and policy gradients from first principles, and is the reference for every reinforcement learning quantity in @sec-training-rl-primer.
- @ross2011reduction is short and states the compounding-error bound and the DAgger remedy together with the assumptions they rest on, including the recoverability condition that @sec-training-recovery-experience examines on hardware.
- @chi2024diffusionpolicy applies diffusion to action chunks on real manipulation tasks, with the receding-horizon execution and the sampling cost that @sec-training-decoder-costs budgets.
- @peng2018sim randomizes dynamics rather than appearance and shows why a policy with memory transfers better, the distinction that decides how wide a randomization range should be.
- @andrychowicz2020learning is the most complete published account of one sim-to-real campaign, including its randomization ablations and the hardware breakage that no simulator priced.
- @ljung1999system is the standard text on fitting models to measured input-output data, with the experiment design that paired probing borrows.

## Problems {#sec-training-problems}

```{python}
#| label: calc-training-problems
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ GIVENS FOR THE END-OF-CHAPTER PROBLEMS (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-training-problems.
# │ Goal:    Hold the givens the problems add to the chapter's cells and guard
# │          each problem's intended answer, which the text does not print.
# │ Show:    the 70/30 demonstration split, the ALOHA arm cell's 50 Hz loop,
# │          the 30-day deadline, 10 integration steps per contact timescale,
# │          the widened friction range, and the 20-run report.
# │ How:     Registry read (Embodied.Manipulator.ALOHA_Bimanual) plus the
# │          earlier cells; answers recomputed in the private solutions.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *

ALOHA = Embodied.Manipulator.ALOHA_Bimanual

class TrainingProblems:
    """Givens that the chapter's problems add beyond the worked examples."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    p_left = 0.70  # category: illustrative (share of demonstrations passing left of the column)
    f_aloha = ALOHA.control_frequency  # category: sourced (ALOHA 50 Hz control loop, Zhao et al. 2023)
    t_deadline_campaign = 30 * day  # category: illustrative (calendar allowed for the from-scratch campaign)
    steps_per_contact = 10  # category: illustrative (integration steps per contact timescale)
    mu_lo, mu_hi = 0.05, 1.5  # category: illustrative (widened friction randomization range)
    n_runs_report = 20  # category: illustrative (physical door runs in the critiqued report)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    p_right = 1 - p_left
    t_step_aloha = (1 / f_aloha).to(millisecond)
    # Intended answers, guarded here and recomputed in the private solutions.
    _yaw_share = p_left - p_right
    _n_renew = math.ceil(((DecoderBudget.t_act + DecoderBudget.t_jitter) / t_step_aloha).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    _rigs_manual = math.ceil((TrialWallClock.t_manual / t_deadline_campaign).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    _rigs_auto = math.ceil((TrialWallClock.t_auto / t_deadline_campaign).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    _v_coast = (LatchContactExploit.f_lim / (LatchContactExploit.k_plate * LatchContactExploit.m_task) ** 0.5).to(meter / second)
    _v_loop = (LatchContactDeadline.f_lim / (LatchContactDeadline.k_plate * LatchContactDeadline.t_contact_loop)).to(meter / second)
    _n_steps_hil = TrialWallClock.n_trials_hil * LatchRewardProblem.n_decisions

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(0.5 < p_left < 1.0, "Problem 1 needs an uneven split with a left majority.")
    check(abs(_yaw_share - 0.4) < 1e-12, f"Problem 1 mean yaw share {_yaw_share}")
    check(abs(t_step_aloha.magnitude - 20.0) < 1e-9, f"ALOHA setpoint step {t_step_aloha}")
    check(DecoderBudget.t_act > t_step_aloha, "Problem 3 needs ACT to miss the arm cell's step.")
    check(_n_renew == 3, f"Problem 3 renewal multiple {_n_renew}")
    check((_rigs_manual, _rigs_auto) == (15, 5), f"Problem 4 rig counts {_rigs_manual}, {_rigs_auto}")
    check(abs(_v_coast.magnitude - 0.0527) < 1e-4, f"Problem 5 coasting ceiling {_v_coast}")
    check(abs(_v_loop.magnitude - 0.125) < 1e-9, f"Problem 5 loop crossover {_v_loop}")
    check(LatchContactDeadline.v_guarded < _v_coast < LatchContactDeadline.v_fast < _v_loop, "Problem 5 ordering")
    check(_n_steps_hil == 240_000, f"Problem 7 steps {_n_steps_hil}")
    check(mu_lo <= AISLE.mu_oil_film < AISLE.mu_dry < mu_hi, "Problem 11 range must bracket the book's floor friction values.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    p_left_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_left, precision=0, style="prose")
    p_right_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_right, precision=0, style="prose")
    aloha_name_str = MarkdownStr(ALOHA.name)
    f_aloha_str = fmt_frequency(f_aloha, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    t_step_aloha_str = fmt_latency(t_step_aloha, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_deadline_campaign_str = fmt_time(t_deadline_campaign, day, precision=0, style="word")
    steps_per_contact_str = fmt_int(steps_per_contact)
    mu_lo_str = fmt(mu_lo, precision=2)
    mu_hi_str = fmt(mu_hi, precision=1)
    n_runs_report_str = fmt_int(n_runs_report)
```

These problems use the running machine's parameters from this chapter's worked examples, with values marked illustrative standing in for measurements as they do there. Each problem names the decision it requires. The tags give the kind of work, from computation through design to critique, and the learning objectives, counted in order, that it assesses.

1. **[Compute, LO2] Unequal modes.** At the column of @sec-training-multimodality-breakdown, suppose the operators pass left in `{python} TrainingProblems.p_left_pct_str` of the demonstrations and right in the remaining `{python} TrainingProblems.p_right_pct_str`, commanding $[v_x, +\omega_z]^\top$ and $[v_x, -\omega_z]^\top$. Find the yaw rate, as a fraction of $\omega_z$, that the squared-error minimizer of @eq-training-mse-minimizer proposes, and the per-dimension median that an $L_1$ loss admits. Repeat both for an even split. Decide in each case whether the loss returns a demonstrated action, and explain why neither loss is a general remedy for mode averaging.
2. **[Compute, LO3] A faster diffusion head.** Keep the encoder time and the `{python} DecoderBudget.k_ddim_str` evaluations of \ref{nbk-training-renewal-slack}. Find the per-evaluation time at which the head fits the `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_step_str` setpoint step synchronously, and the per-evaluation time at which it runs asynchronously with the `{python} DecoderBudget.t_jitter_str` jitter allowance free inside the `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_chunk_str` renewal period, each as a fraction of the stipulated `{python} DecoderBudget.t_eval_str`. Then find the inference time of a head distilled to half the evaluations at the stipulated cost. Decide which deadline each change meets.
3. **[Compute, LO3] ACT on a bimanual arm cell.** The `{python} TrainingProblems.aloha_name_str`, a stationary two-arm cell, closes its control loop at `{python} TrainingProblems.f_aloha_str`, a `{python} TrainingProblems.t_step_aloha_str` setpoint step, and the registry lists the same processor as the running machine's. Assume that ACT keeps its `{python} DecoderBudget.t_act_str` P99 inference there (illustrative) and that the lease rule keeps its `{python} DecoderBudget.t_jitter_str` jitter allowance. Decide whether ACT can run synchronously. If it cannot, find the shortest renewal period that is a whole number of setpoint steps and leaves the jitter allowance free, the slack it leaves, and how many setpoints of a `{python} DecoderBudget.horizon_str`-step chunk play between renewals. State which fields of the policy inference contract change when the checkpoint moves to this cell.
4. **[Compute, LO5] Rigs or a reset fixture.** A team must finish the from-scratch campaign of \ref{nbk-training-reset-wall} within `{python} TrainingProblems.t_deadline_campaign_str`. Using @eq-training-trial-wall-clock, find the number of identical rigs it needs with manual resets and with automated resets, and the drivetrain load reversals in each case. Then find how many trials the `{python} TrialWallClock.t_hil_max_str` demonstration-seeded campaign of @sec-training-real-world-rl admits with manual resets, against the `{python} TrialWallClock.n_trials_hil_str` it admits with automated ones. Decide whether the reset fixture or additional rigs is the better investment for each regime.
5. **[Compute, LO4] Two approach ceilings.** From the inputs of \ref{nbk-training-soft-spring-exploit}, find the highest speed at which a rigid robot coasting into the plate stays within the `{python} LatchContactExploit.f_lim_str` limit (@eq-training-impact-peak), and the speed at which the contact yield deadline of @eq-training-contact-yield-deadline equals the `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_contact_loop_str` contact-loop response. Decide which model binds, what fraction of the limit the guarded approach reaches under it, and what approach ceiling the permission path should enforce until the robot-side stiffness is measured.
6. **[Compute, LO4] Stiffening the simulated spring.** The contact timescale $\sqrt{m/k}$ is `{python} LatchContactExploit.t_contact_sim_str` against the penalty spring and `{python} LatchContactExploit.t_contact_plate_str` against the plate (@sec-training-policy-manifest). Suppose the integrator needs `{python} TrainingProblems.steps_per_contact_str` steps per contact timescale (illustrative), that the latch simulator reaches the reported throughput of @sec-training-parallel-simulation at the timestep that resolves the soft spring, and that its cost per policy step scales with the number of physics steps. Find both timesteps and the duration of the `{python} ParallelSimBudget.latch_steps_str`-step latch campaign once the spring matches the plate, and compare it with the `{python} TrialWallClock.t_auto_days_str` automated-reset calendar. Decide whether contact fidelity or throughput limits the simulated route.
7. **[Compute, LO5] Exposure of a demonstration-seeded campaign.** Suppose each of the `{python} TrialWallClock.n_trials_hil_str` trials of the `{python} TrialWallClock.t_hil_max_str` campaign runs `{python} LatchRewardProblem.n_decisions_str` decisions at `{python} LatchRewardProblem.t_step_str`, and `{python} LatchResidualExposure.frac_exceed_pct_str` of decisions cross the `{python} LatchResidualExposure.f_trip_str` tripwire, as in the `latch-res-03` example. Find the decision count, the active time, and the above-tripwire samples, and compare them with the `{python} LatchResidualExposure.n_steps_str` steps of `latch-res-03`. State what event segmentation must establish before these samples can be charged against a drivetrain life model.
8. **[Design, LO1] A regime for the negatively displaced plate.** `latch-bc-recovery-02` covers only the positive displacement. Choose the regime that should supply competence at the negative displacement from four candidates: a second recovery-demonstration campaign; demonstration-seeded reinforcement learning on the machine (`{python} TrialWallClock.n_trials_hil_str` trials and `{python} TrialWallClock.n_reversals_hil_str` load reversals at the upper end of its range); reinforcement learning in the existing simulator, whose spring is `{python} LatchContactExploit.plate_over_sim_mult_str` softer than the plate and whose omission log holds two open entries; and offline reinforcement learning on the retained archive. For each, state the experience it supplies, the dependency it leaves, and the evidence required before the new cell enters a declared ODD. State how the choice changes if the correction depends on force cues that a teleoperator cannot perceive.
9. **[Design, LO5] Authority for `latch-res-03`.** Specify the gate condition, the magnitude and slew limits, and the regression suite that must pass before the residual of @eq-training-gated-residual receives authority. For each limit, name the measurement that must supply its value, and identify which of those measurements the chapter has not yet made. Decide whether the residual may be trained on the machine while the omission log still holds the soft-spring entry.
10. **[Design, LO6] The recovery manifest.** Write each field of @tbl-06-training-schema for `latch-bc-recovery-02`. Count its supported cells and known absences on the `{python} PretrainSupport.n_cells_str`-cell scenario ledger, state its declared ODD, and name the regression evidence its qualification request must carry for the nominal cell.
11. **[Critique, LO4] Widening the friction range.** A team reports that widening friction randomization to [`{python} TrainingProblems.mu_lo_str`, `{python} TrainingProblems.mu_hi_str`] fixed latch transfer, citing `{python} TrainingProblems.n_runs_report_str` successful physical door runs at the nominal plate. Evaluate the claim. Identify the evidence that would distinguish a genuine fix from a conservative compromise that masks an omitted mechanism, state what the policy's memory changes about that judgment, and decide which entries of the omission log the report can close.
12. **[Critique, LO1, LO6] Borrowed competence.** A team post-trains the machine's `{python} PretrainSupport.base_name_str` intent model on the latch campaign, observes plausible behavior at both plate displacements, and proposes a declared ODD covering all `{python} PretrainSupport.n_cells_str` cells because the `{python} PretrainSupport.n_pretrain_str` pretraining episodes include many doors. Critique the proposal against the join of @sec-data-policy-coverage, name the manifest fields that must record the base, and state what the candidate's decoder must show against the latch's deadlines before it may propose motion. Decide the declared ODD.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From policy manifests to evidence"}
How much can a finite run of clean trials establish about a checkpoint whose manifest already limits where it may be trusted? @Sec-evaluation takes the policy manifest as its input. Its illustrative campaign begins with twenty nominal door runs of `latch-bc-01` and asks what that finite sample establishes. A separate stipulated branch takes `latch-bc-recovery-02` through nominal regression and displaced-plate qualification, showing what additional evidence would support useful recovery under the guarded approach.
:::
